title: Longing for sight
hook: Guru Ram Das's hymns long for the sight of the Beloved and the True Guru (Sri Rag M4, ang 40)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ghorian, Guru Ram Das's wedding horse songs: the body a horse the Lord made, the soul riding home. Your line was ride to the beloved. What kind thing did you give your horse? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

What does missing someone actually want? Not news. You can have all the news in the world about a person far away, what they ate, where they went, how the weather is, and the ache stays exactly where it was. What it wants is to see them. The face. The door opening and there they are. Earlier on this path we heard young Arjan's letters home, longing to see his father. Today we hear the father. Guru Ram Das has hymns full of that same ache, and the word at the center of them is sight.
screen: `NOT NEWS. THE FACE.` → `ARJAN'S LETTERS, LONGING.` → `NOW THE FATHER'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's one, from Sri Rag, paraphrased. In my mind and body, the pain of separation is great. How will my Beloved come home and meet me? When I see my Lord, seeing him, the pain goes away. I go and ask my friends: how can I meet the Lord? And the refrain: O my True Guru, without you I have no other. Four things are in there. First, the word for that pain, birha, the ache of being apart from someone you love. The hymn doesn't hide it or hurry past it. It says it's great, and it's in the mind and the body both. Second, the cure. Not a better argument. Seeing. When I see my Lord, the pain goes. Sikhs call that seeing darsan: a glimpse of the beloved, of the Guru, of the Lord. Third, the friends. Longing doesn't sit alone at home. It goes out and asks the people who have met the Beloved how they did it. That's one picture of what the sangat is for. Fourth, the refrain turns to the Guru: without you, I have no other. The longing for God and the longing for the Guru run through the same hymn, because in Sikh teaching it's the Guru who shows the way to that sight. Notice what the hymn trusts. It doesn't treat longing as a problem to get over. The ache is part of the road. It's what sends you out the door asking.
screen: `BIRHA: THE ACHE OF BEING APART.` · `DARSAN: SEEING HEALS IT.` · `ASK THE FRIENDS WHO HAVE MET.` · `WITHOUT YOU, I HAVE NO OTHER.` · then, large: `LONGING FOR SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an image of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the gurdwara Sikhs travel to for darsan. Find a photo if you can, and in the sit, just look: the water, the reflection, the people walking around. If you can't find one, let a place or a face you long to see come to mind instead, and look at it gently. No need to fix the longing. Let it be there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Longing for sight. Guru Ram Das's ache of separation, healed by seeing: darsan of the Beloved, and the True Guru without whom there is no other. Today's word.
Your line: longing for sight. When you miss someone today, don't brush it off. Let it send you to ask, to call, or to go and see. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of going for darsan of the Guru Granth Sahib at the gurdwara and of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and Guru Ram Das's hymns of longing are sung in kirtan.

fork.reveal: I go and ask my friends: how can I meet the Lord? longing goes looking for company.

original.note: sight, a glimpse of the beloved: of the Guru, of the Lord; what the longing in these hymns wants.

trapdoor: what you thought: longing is a feeling to get past.
what it means: in the hymn, longing is the road; it sends you asking, and sight heals it.
